name: Sulisobenzone
lead: Sulisobenzone, also called benzophenone-4 (BP-4), is a water-soluble organic UV filter that absorbs UVB and short-wave UVA light [1]. People encounter it as an ingredient in some sunscreens, where it helps protect skin from sun-driven tanning, burning, uneven pigment and photoageing, and in some hair products, where it is used to protect colour and structure [1][8]. Its sodium salt is called benzophenone-5 [1].

For appearance, sunscreen filters matter because ultraviolet exposure is a main driver of visible skin ageing and pigment change, and dermatology-minded looksmaxxing discussions regularly put daily broad-spectrum sunscreen near the top of a routine. Sulisobenzone is one of the older filters in that toolbox; a 1983 randomized trial included it among the agents compared for UVA protection [6].

Published work on sulisobenzone covers regulatory safety review, contact allergy testing, skin absorption modelling and its presence in the environment. The European Commission's scientific committee on consumer safety has issued an opinion on it, and environmental studies have found it among the most abundant UV filters in river water [4][2].
infobox: SCCS: safe up to 5% as UV filter in sunscreen and other listed products [4]

paras: Sulisobenzone is an ingredient in some sunscreens, where it absorbs UVB and UVA [1]. Wikipedia groups it among the UVA plus UVB filters that are approved by one or more regulators without detailing particular approvals [1].

A 1993 article in the International Journal of Cosmetic Science reviewed UV filters for hair protection, the topic behind the use of UV filters in hair products to limit light-driven damage to colour and structure [8]. Its water solubility makes it easier to put into aqueous hair products than oil-soluble benzophenones [1].

Sulisobenzone has the formula C14H12O6S and a molar mass of about 308 g/mol. It is a light-tan powder that melts at about 145 C and dissolves in water at roughly 1 g per 4 mL [1]. The sulfonic acid group on the benzophenone core is what makes it far more water-soluble than other benzophenones such as oxybenzone [1]. The preferred IUPAC name is 5-benzoyl-4-hydroxy-2-methoxybenzene-1-sulfonic acid [1].

The EU's Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety (SCCS) published an opinion on benzophenone-4 (SCCS/1660/23). It concluded that BP-4 is safe as a UV filter up to a maximum concentration of 5 percent in sunscreen and in leave-on and rinse-off products based on total dermal aggregate exposure, and that the same applies to lipstick, sunscreen propellant and pump spray. Its use as a light stabiliser should stay within 5 percent including its use as a filter. The assessment did not cover environmental safety [4].

A 2025 review of 35 in vitro skin permeation papers on the 12 most-used organic UV filters estimated blood and skin concentrations. Of the five filters that penetrated skin as the parent compound, benzophenone-4 had the highest estimated blood concentration (419 mg/L), but the estimates overshot reported in vivo results by up to 100 times and the authors noted inconsistent methods across studies [3]. An earlier stripping study in 21 women examined how much of two sunscreen agents, including a benzophenone, remained in the stratum corneum over 1 to 7 hours [7].

In a 15-year clinic experience of 402 patients with suspected photosensitivity, 80 (20 percent) had allergic or photoallergic contact dermatitis to at least one UV absorber. Benzophenone-4 produced no allergic or photoallergic reactions among the ten absorbers tested from 1989 onward, whereas benzophenone-3 produced 3 allergic and 9 photoallergic reactions [10]. A 2026 review of allergic contact dermatitis to personal care products nevertheless lists benzophenone-4 among emerging allergens, alongside octocrylene [5]. The North American Contact Dermatitis Group patch-test report for 2013 to 2014 also covers UV-filter allergens [11].

A Swiss monitoring study sampled river water above and below wastewater plants and found BP-4 at the highest concentrations of four detected UV filters, ahead of BP-3, 4-MBC and EHMC [2]. A survey of surface waters in eight cities in four countries and the North American Arctic reported on twelve organic UV filters and a risk assessment [12], and a study of wastewater plants examined seasonal occurrence and removal [13]. Filters as a class have also been tested for hormone-like activity: a fish study compared yeast and in vivo estrogenic activity of 23 UV filters [14]. Sulisobenzone has also been reported in a structural biology study as an inhibitor of the bacterial transcription factor Cra, a laboratory finding unrelated to skin use [15].

A 1983 randomized trial of topical protection against long-wave UVA in the setting of psoralen plus UVA therapy found that a PABA ester plus oxybenzone preparation was superior to PABA or sulisobenzone alone in protecting skin from methoxsalen-induced UVA phototoxicity after a water challenge [6].

Other human data are about safety rather than appearance: patch and photopatch testing for allergy [10][11], a double-blind assessment of the irritant potential of sunscreen dilutions used in photopatch testing [16], and skin-stripping absorption work [7]. No published trial examines sulisobenzone as a stand-alone cosmetic treatment.

timeline.event: A randomized trial compares sulisobenzone with PABA and a PABA ester plus oxybenzone for UVA protection in PUVA patients [6].

SCCS publishes its opinion on benzophenone-4 [4].

card.summary: A water-soluble benzophenone UV filter (BP-4) used in sunscreens and hair products, studied mostly as an environmental contaminant.
card.note: Research is mainly environmental, not clinical.

quick.overview:
Sulisobenzone (benzophenone-4) is a UV filter that absorbs UVB and short UVA. Unlike other benzophenones it dissolves in water, so it also appears in some hair products.
Most published work on it concerns its presence in rivers and wastewater rather than human trials.
quick.mechanism: It absorbs ultraviolet light through its benzophenone structure; the sulfonic acid group makes it water-soluble.
quick.risks: There are no dedicated human safety trials. Environmental studies report it in surface water, and UV filters as a class have been tested for hormone-like activity in cells and fish.

chain: Less sunburn, tanning and pigment change over time
angle.text: Sulisobenzone is used as a UV filter in sunscreens, so skin receives less of the ultraviolet light that causes burning, tanning and visible photoageing. Because it is water-soluble it can also be formulated into hair products to help protect colour.
